lead: This unit builds the vocabulary the rest of the subject runs on: what a cloud is, where it came from, what it is made of, and who owns what inside it. After these nine chapters you can define a cloud against the standard five characteristics, place any service on the reference model, name its service and deployment model, and count what it costs.
about: This unit gives you the words and the map that the rest of the subject uses. Chapter 1.1 follows the line from clusters to grids to utility billing to the cloud. Chapter 1.2 separates parallel from distributed computing and orders the eras of computing. Chapter 1.3 fixes the standard definition and its five characteristics; 1.4 sets the benefits against the risks. Chapter 1.5 draws the layered reference model, and 1.6 cuts that same stack at three heights to get IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. Chapter 1.7 asks who should own the hardware, 1.8 names the actors and counts the money, and 1.9 pushes the same ideas to the edge of the network and into mobile devices.

chapters.idea: The cloud is the commercial end of a forty-year habit: pooling many computers so that one job can use all of them and each user pays only for what they use.
chapters.depth: Three earlier forms. Cluster computing: many identical machines in one room, one owner, one fast local network, one administrator, presented as a single system; used for rendering and simulation. Grid computing: machines of different kinds in different organisations, joined by middleware and a resource broker, shared through a virtual organisation; a few syllabi call this 'historical developments' and only a few universities teach the middleware layer (Globus-style toolkits) in detail. Utility computing: computing sold by the meter, the way electricity is sold. Then the cloud, which adds self-service and elasticity on top of utility billing. Close with a timeline: mainframe time-sharing, cluster, grid, utility, cloud.

figure.title: From pooled machines to the cloud
figure.aria: A left-to-right chain of five stages, mainframe time-sharing, cluster, grid, utility computing and cloud, with the final step that adds self-service picked out.

chapters.example: A ticket-booking site needs 300 servers for 5 days each month and 20 servers for the other days. Buying costs ₹80,000 per server for 300 servers, plus ₹3,00,000 per month to run them. Renting costs ₹30 per server-hour, charged only for servers that are switched on. Compare the first 12 months. Rented: peak 300 × 5 × 24 = 36,000 server-hours; off-peak 20 × 20 × 24 = 9,600 server-hours; total 45,600 × ₹30 = ₹13,68,000 per month, or ₹1,64,16,000 for 12 months. Bought: 300 × ₹80,000 = ₹2,40,00,000 once, plus 12 × ₹3,00,000 = ₹36,00,000 running, total ₹2,76,00,000. Renting saves ₹1,11,84,000 because the bought servers sit idle for 19 days a month.
chapters.trap: Writing 'grid' and 'cluster' as the same thing. Both run a job across many machines, but a cluster has one owner and one network, while a grid crosses organisational boundaries and needs middleware to negotiate access.
chapters.leave: The inside of a hypervisor and virtual machine mechanics to Unit 3. Scaling and load balancing to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Parallel computing splits one job across processors that can share data cheaply; distributed computing joins independent computers that share nothing but a network and a message, and the cloud is a distributed system wrapped in a business layer.
chapters.depth: Elements of parallel computing: a set of processors, a memory they can all reach or messages between them, and an interconnection network. Flynn's four classes (single instruction single data, single instruction multiple data, multiple instruction single data, multiple instruction multiple data); some syllabi call this 'classification of parallel systems'. Shared-memory versus message-passing. Speedup S = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/n), where p is the fraction of the work that can run in parallel and n is the number of processors. Distributed computing proper: no global clock, partial failure, independent administration, concurrency, and the transparency the user is promised. Eras of computing: batch mainframe, time-sharing terminals, personal computer, client-server and web, then cloud and mobile. One line on parallelisation in the cloud (task parallelism and data parallelism); the programming models belong to Unit 5.

figure.aria: Three curves of speedup against processor count, each rising and then flattening at the ceiling set by its parallel fraction.

chapters.example: A job has 80% of its work that can run in parallel, so p = 0.8. With n = 4 processors, S = 1 / (0.2 + 0.8/4) = 1/0.4 = 2.5 times. With n = 16, S = 1 / (0.2 + 0.8/16) = 1/0.25 = 4.0 times. With n = 1,000, S = 1 / (0.2 + 0.0008) ≈ 4.98, so the ceiling is 1/0.2 = 5 times no matter how many processors you buy. The other 20% is the serial part and it sets the bill you can never recover.
chapters.trap: Quoting Amdahl's law with n as the number of tasks instead of the number of processors, and forgetting to state the ceiling 1/(1 − p). Also answering 'many machines' when asked for the difference between parallel and distributed: the difference is shared memory versus a network, and one clock versus no global clock.
chapters.leave: MapReduce, Spark and task graphs to Unit 5. Scheduling policies to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: One standard definition replaces the marketing word 'cloud' with a test: five essential characteristics, all of which must hold at once.
chapters.depth: The standard definition (NIST SP 800-145, quoted in paraphrase): a model for enabling on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources that can be provisioned and released with minimal management effort. The five essential characteristics, each examined: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling (multitenancy), rapid elasticity, measured service. Virtualisation as the mechanism that makes pooling possible, kept brief because Unit 3 owns it. The three service models and four deployment models are named only, since chapters 1.6 and 1.7 cover them. Some syllabi call the whole set 'defining a cloud' or 'characteristics and benefits'.

figure.title: The five-characteristic test
figure.aria: A definition box at the top branching into five characteristic boxes: self-service, network access, pooling, elasticity and measured service, with elasticity picked out.

chapters.example: A college offers students a login on one server in the campus data centre, billed as a flat ₹500 per student per year, reachable only from inside the campus Wi-Fi, with accounts created by emailing the administrator. Test it against the five characteristics. Self-service: no, it needs a human. Broad network access: no, campus Wi-Fi only. Resource pooling: partly, one machine, many users. Rapid elasticity: no, the class of 60 cannot get 600 machines in 6 minutes. Measured service: partly, flat fee, not metered per second. Two partial out of five, so it is a hosted service, not a cloud.
chapters.trap: Calling any virtual machine a cloud. A VM on your laptop has pooling of hardware but none of self-service, broad access, elasticity or metering. Answer with all five characteristics, then judge.
chapters.leave: The virtualisation machinery to Unit 3. The full service and deployment models to chapters 1.6 and 1.7 below.

chapters.idea: Cloud computing trades capital cost and direct control for operating cost and convenience, and every benefit it gives has a matching risk on the other side of the ledger.
chapters.depth: Benefits: capital cost becomes operating cost, elasticity removes over-provisioning, faster time to start, global reach from one region away, provider handles patching and redundancy, focus on the core business. Risks and challenges: vendor lock-in, data security and privacy, regulatory compliance and data location, outage and dependency on the link, latency for far regions, hidden egress and storage charges, limited low-level control, tenant isolation in shared hardware, skills gap. A short list of common threat types (data breach, account hijack, insecure interface, denial of service) with the detail handed to Unit 6. Finish with a benefit-to-risk table and the mitigation for each risk.

figure.aria: A two-branch tree: benefits such as avoiding capital cost, elastic scale and global reach on one side, risks such as lock-in, data loss and unexpected bills on the other.

chapters.example: A startup stores 1 TB of photos in the cloud at ₹2 per GB per month and serves 3 TB of downloads each month at ₹6.50 per GB. Compute the bill and the share of it that walks out the door. Storage: 1 TB = 1,024 GB × ₹2 = ₹2,048. Download: 3 TB = 3,072 GB × ₹6.50 = ₹19,968. Total = ₹22,016 per month, of which download is 19,968/22,016 = 90.7%. If a video goes viral and downloads double, the bill becomes ₹2,048 + ₹39,936 = ₹41,984 while stored data has not changed at all.
chapters.trap: Listing benefits and stopping, when the question asks for risks and challenges too. The other trap is calling egress charges a security risk: they are a cost risk, and exams mark the category.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.3 to 1.4 of the definition, so that benefits map to characteristics.
chapters.leave: Attack vectors and controls to Unit 6. Cost and billing models to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The architecture is a stack of layers, from physical hardware up to the application, with management, security and governance cutting across every layer; the reference model also has an actor view, which chapter 1.8 covers.
chapters.depth: Provider side versus consumer side. Layers bottom up: physical (data centres, servers, storage, network), virtualisation (hypervisor, virtual machines, virtual networks), platform (operating system, runtime, middleware, databases), application. Cross-cutting concerns that touch all four layers: security, management (resource, service, SLA), governance. Say clearly that the actor view (consumer, provider, broker, auditor, carrier) is the second half of the reference model and is chapter 1.8. Some syllabi call all of this the 'cloud computing architectural framework'; the layered diagram is the answer to write.

figure.aria: A four-layer stack running from the application at the top down to physical servers at the bottom, with control passing from the consumer near the top to the provider near the bottom.

chapters.example: A college web app runs on 4 virtual machines behind 1 load balancer, with a managed database of 200 GB and 500 GB of object storage for lecture videos. Place all six elements on the layered model and say who manages each when the site is bought as infrastructure as a service. Load balancer and 4 VMs: virtualisation layer, the provider runs the hypervisor, the college manages the operating system and everything above it. Managed database: platform layer, provider handles patching and backup. 500 GB object storage: physical storage layer made shared, provider manages. Cross-cutting management and security apply to all six.
chapters.trap: Drawing only the four layers and forgetting the cross-cutting security and management bands; and confusing this layered architecture with the actor-based reference model. Marks are lost for leaving either out.
chapters.leave: Who each service model covers to chapter 1.6. AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and OpenStack stacks to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Infrastructure, platform and software as a service are the same stack cut at three heights, so the cut point decides what you rent, what you must manage and what you pay for.
chapters.depth: IaaS: raw virtual machines, storage and networks; you own the operating system upward; billed per hour or second; example, a rented virtual server. PaaS: you supply code and configuration, the provider supplies the runtime, middleware, OS and scaling; example, pushing a Python web app and never seeing a server. SaaS: the whole application over a browser; example, webmail or a billing service; billed per user per month. The management responsibility matrix laid out for all three. The XaaS tail (functions, database, storage, desktop as a service); only a few universities teach the full list, so cover functions as a service in three lines and stop. Name a common use case for each model, without naming a college or a vendor's price list.

figure.title: Who manages each layer
figure.aria: A table of the three service models against five layers, showing the provider taking over more layers as you move from infrastructure to platform to software as a service.

chapters.example: A college has 300 students who need mail, and asks whether a rented mail service at ₹120 per student per year beats running its own mail server on one virtual machine at ₹2,400 per month plus 4 hours of administrator time per month at ₹600 per hour. Rented: 300 × ₹120 = ₹36,000 per year. Self-run: VM 12 × ₹2,400 = ₹28,800, plus admin 12 × 4 × ₹600 = ₹28,800, total ₹57,600 per year. Rented wins by ₹21,600 per year, and the college also stops patching a mail server, which is the software-as-a-service argument in one line.
chapters.trap: Saying that in PaaS 'you manage nothing' - you still manage the application, its configuration and its data. The other trap is calling serverless a fourth classical model; it is a form of XaaS sitting on top of platform as a service.
chapters.leave: Virtual machines, containers and hypervisors to Unit 3. Live provider stacks to Unit 5. Per-second metering detail to chapter 1.8.

chapters.idea: The deployment model answers who owns the hardware and who shares it, which is a different question from what is being sold as a service.
chapters.depth: Public: the provider owns the hardware and sells to anyone, many tenants share it. Private: one organisation owns or leases the whole pool, on its own premises or hosted; control and compliance, but you carry the capital cost. Hybrid: a private core with public capacity on tap, joined by secure links; cloud bursting is the usual example - private servers run the base load, public servers take the spike. Community: several organisations with a shared concern pool the hardware, such as a group of colleges sharing an examination portal. Also one line on virtual private cloud (a private slice carved out of public hardware) and multi-cloud; only a few universities teach federated and intercloud arrangements. Give a selection table: data sensitivity, regulation, load shape, skill, budget.

figure.aria: Two overlapping circles for private and public clouds, with the hybrid model sitting in the overlap where a private workload bursts into public capacity.

chapters.example: A hospital chain keeps patient records that must stay on its own premises. Its appointment site normally takes 200 requests per second but sees 2,000 per second for 3 days during a health camp. Its private data centre can serve 300 requests per second. Buying 10 more servers to cover the peak costs ₹80,000 each, ₹8,00,000, and for 362 days a year they do nothing. Bursting those 10 servers into the public cloud for 3 days at ₹30 per server-hour costs 10 × 72 × ₹30 = ₹21,600. Hybrid is chosen: records stay private, the appointment site bursts outward.
chapters.trap: Calling any server room a private cloud. It still needs pooling, self-service, elasticity and metering; without them it is traditional hosting. Also, hybrid is not 'any two clouds' - the two parts must be joined and the workload must move between them.
chapters.leave: Tenant isolation and segmentation to Unit 6. Federated and intercloud to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Around one cloud sit named roles with named responsibilities, boundaries that say who controls what, and a meter that turns usage into money.
chapters.depth: The actor view of the reference model: consumer, provider, auditor (checks logs and compliance independently), broker (aggregates and resells services), carrier (provides the connection). Boundaries: the organisational boundary (who legally owns the data), the trust boundary (what one party can see and change), and the responsibility boundary inherited from chapter 1.6. Economics: capital expense versus operating expense, economies of scale, pay-per-use metering (per second, per GB-month, per million requests), on-demand versus reserved pricing, total cost of ownership including people time. Define SLA and SLO here: an SLA is the contract that names the service, its measurable targets, and the penalties; an SLO is one target inside it, for example 99.9% availability in a month allows at most 43 minutes of downtime. List what common providers sell and their stacks in one line each (compute, storage, managed database, and an open-source stack such as OpenStack), with the detail left to Unit 5.

figure.aria: Five actors drawn as a graph: the consumer buys from the provider, the broker resells to the consumer, the auditor checks the provider, and the carrier supplies the network link.

chapters.example: An app runs 4 virtual machines at ₹6 per VM-hour, 24 hours a day, through a 30-day month, keeps 500 GB of storage at ₹2 per GB per month, and serves 20 million requests at ₹0.5 per million. On-demand bill: compute 4 × 720 hours = 2,880 VM-hours × ₹6 = ₹17,280; storage 500 × ₹2 = ₹1,000; requests 20 × ₹0.5 = ₹10; total ₹18,290 per month. A one-year reserved contract takes 40% off compute: 17,280 × 0.6 = ₹10,368, new total ₹11,378, saving ₹6,912 per month or ₹82,944 per year for the same 4 virtual machines.
chapters.trap: Leaving out the auditor and the broker, which most answers forget, and swapping SLA with SLO. An SLA is the contract; an SLO is one measured target inside it. Also, cost is not price: cost includes staff time and migration.
chapters.leave: Monitoring, logging and identity to Unit 6. SLA monitoring and breach handling to Unit 2. Detailed cost models to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: When delay or connectivity is the binding limit, the computation walks towards the user: to a node at the edge of the network, or into a mobile cloud that offloads from the phone.
chapters.depth: Edge computing: computation placed close to where the data is produced, small nodes with limited power, managed from the cloud as one fleet; the point is milliseconds and backhaul saving. Fog computing is the layer between the edge and the cloud - the term comes from the networking world; only a few universities use the word fog, so define it in two lines. Mobile cloud computing: the phone, the radio network and the cloud working together, with offloading decisions based on energy, delay and bandwidth; cloudlets as small nearby data centres; challenges of intermittent links, battery, heterogeneity and data cost on mobile plans. Where each paradigm wins, and why the cloud does not disappear: long jobs, training, archives stay in the data centre.

figure.title: Where the work runs
figure.aria: A chain from a camera to a nearby edge node, then a regional fog node, then a distant cloud data centre, with round-trip delay growing at each step and the edge link highlighted.

chapters.example: A toll-gate number-plate reader must answer within 50 ms. On the camera itself the model takes 90 ms, too slow. In the cloud, 60 ms round trip plus 20 ms of inference is 80 ms, also too slow. On an edge node 5 ms away, 5 + 20 = 25 ms, which fits with 25 ms to spare. The link matters too: 1,000 cameras sending a 2 MB frame twice a second is 4,000 MB per second, or 32 Gbit/s of backhaul. Send only alerts instead, one 50 KB alert per camera every 10 seconds, and the link carries 100 × 50 KB = 5 MB per second, or 40 Mbit/s.
chapters.trap: Calling any nearby server 'edge'. An edge node is defined by being close to the data source and managed as part of the cloud fleet, not by being small. The second trap is treating mobile cloud computing as a website opened on a phone.
chapters.leave: VM migration, containers and virtual clusters to Unit 3. Radio and data-centre network technology to Unit 2.
